Records and conversion
A payment in crypto is still a payment you have to plan for. Decide how much you will hold before it arrives, and set the tax money aside either way.
Yield on the runway?
Runway
Build the runway before chasing yield. A yield offer is not a reason to put money you may need soon into an unaudited product.
The tax money in the corner
Tax
Tax money is not optional capital. If it is owed in two months, it stays where it can be paid.
The client pays late
Cash flow

You are choosing a **standing plan** for months 6 and 7, not predicting this month's gap. The plan is scored on the order it puts your safety nets in: spend less or use your own emergency savings first, and a 2%-a-month card last. That is judged from what you hold now. It does not depend on whether a gap actually appears, and nothing later is used to score it.
A late client tests cash flow. Use the runway or trim spending before borrowing at 2% a month, and notice that holding the invoice in USDC left the business with less cash exactly when it was needed.
Sign here to release your invoice
Wallet safety
Money is rarely "released" by signing or paying a stranger. When a request is unsolicited and urgent, verify it independently.
Catching up on records
Records
Records are cheap while you are small and expensive later. Keep a log of every crypto receipt and conversion, and decide how future payments will arrive.
The vault reports an exploit
Incidents
After an incident, protect the runway first and do not add money to recoup a loss. No recovery is guaranteed, and nothing in this story depends on one.

blurb: A freelance designer, 38, with lumpy income: paid in USDC, a late client, a scam message and an exploited vault.
intro: Marcus Rivera, 38, freelance designer. His income is lumpy, so he keeps three ring-fenced pools: runway (emergency savings), tax, and optional (experiments). Business cash $2,400, personal checking $900, emergency savings $2,600, no crypto, no debt. A business credit card (limit $1,500, 2% a month) is unused.
name: Marcus Rivera
plan: Stablecoin limit (a stablecoin is a crypto token designed to stay worth $1, such as USDC): hold no more than $1,500 in USDC at a time.
Runway: emergency savings target $6,000 (two months of personal spending). He has $2,600. Runway money is not for yield.

Tax reserve is committed money. It is for the next estimated payment, not for experiments. Real estimated-tax dates are April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15; this story uses a simplified schedule and an assumed set-aside rate.
Operating buffer: about $1,500 stays in business cash. Cash above it is surplus that can be moved.
Records: log every crypto receipt and every conversion.
Wallet safety: never sign an unsolicited request, and never pay a fee to "release" money.
